chunks: And with this chain of narrators, he said:

A man invited one of the Banu Hashim to single combat (al-baraz), but he declined to fight him. Ali (peace be upon him) said to him, 'What prevented you from fighting him?' He said, 'He was the horseman (champion) of the Arabs, and I feared that he would overpower me.' Ali (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Indeed, he has been unjust/aggressive towards you. And if you had fought him, you would have overcome him. And if a mountain were to be unjust/aggressive towards another mountain, the aggressive one would perish.'

key_terms.الْبَاغِي: The one who is aggressive or unjust; the one who initiates the transgression
key_terms.الْبِرَاز: Single combat or duel, specifically between two champions
key_terms.بَغَى: To be unjust, aggressive, or transgress; here referring to initiating conflict unjustly
key_terms.فَارِسَ الْعَرَبِ: The horseman/champion of the Arabs, denoting a renowned warrior

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of al-baraz and the lesson of 'the mountain that is unjust perishes' in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Thawab al-A'mal* highlights the virtue of *bagh* (aggression/injustice) as a spiritual and physical weakness, even against formidable opponents like the 'champion of the Arabs.' Imam Ali (AS) uses the metaphor of mountains to illustrate that the aggressor inevitably perishes, reinforcing the Shia theological principle that divine support favors the righteous over the tyrannical, regardless of worldly power. This incident serves as a practical lesson in courage and trust in God (*tawakkul*) when facing unjust challenges.

en.sayed-athar-husain-rizvi-&-sayed-maqs: 5. And from the previous chain who said: “
If he has done injustice to you, you should have fought with him and overpowered him, because if a mountain does injustice to another, Allah destroys the unjust mountain.”
